title: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])
word: From the rising of the sun
hook: God stoops down to lift the poor from the dust

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vespers, and a priest for ever like Melchisedech. Your line was a priest for ever. Did you stop at sunset? Today, a psalm that runs from sunrise to sunset. Day one hundred eighty.

Think about the sun for a second. Right now, somewhere on earth, it's rising. Somewhere else it's setting. It's always coming up on someone's morning. Which means that at every single moment, someone somewhere is waking up, and someone is going to bed. A short psalm takes that fact and turns it into praise that never stops, a relay around the planet. And then, halfway through, it looks down from the sky, all the way down to the garbage heap at the edge of town.
screen: `ALWAYS SOMEONE'S SUNRISE.` → `PRAISE THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `DOWN TO THE GARBAGE HEAP.`

segments.voice: Psalm 112 in the Douay, 113 in most Bibles. It opens: "Praise the Lord, ye children: praise ye the name of the Lord." Children here follows the Latin, pueri, a word that can also mean servants, and the Hebrew does say servants: you who serve the Lord. Then the sun: "From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same, the name of the Lord is worthy of praise." East to west, morning to night. Then it climbs as high as it can go. God is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens. Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high? And then the great surprise. This God looks down, on the low things in heaven and in earth. And the psalm keeps going down: "Raising up the needy from the earth, and lifting up the poor out of the dunghill: That he may place him with princes, with the princes of his people." The dunghill was the town dump, where the poorest people slept and begged. The God above the heavens stoops all the way down to the dump and seats someone from there at the royal table. Then one more: the woman who couldn't have children is made the joyful mother of a household. If that sounds familiar, it should. Hannah sings nearly the same lines about the poor and the dunghill when her son is born, and Mary sings the same turning-over of the world in the Magnificat. This psalm begins the Hallel, the psalms of praise Jews sing at Passover. Many think these were the hymn Jesus and his friends sang at the Last Supper before going out to the Mount of Olives.
screen: `YE CHILDREN, YE SERVANTS.` · `FROM SUNRISE TO SUNSET.` · `OUT OF THE DUNGHILL, TO PRINCES.` · `HANNAH, MARY, THE HALLEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lift someone's spirits today. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who's low right now: discouraged, overlooked, stuck, sitting on their own small dunghill. Picture them. Now think of one small thing that might lift them a little: a message, a call, a compliment that's true, a coffee, an invitation to sit at your table. If you pray, you can pray for them in the psalm's words: raising up the needy. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and decide on your one small thing. The bell holds the time.
From the rising of the sun. Praise running around the world all day, to the God who stoops to lift the poor. Today's word.
screen: `FROM THE RISING OF THE SUN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he raises the needy. Today, do the one small thing you chose for that person, before the sun goes down. Day one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 112 [113] at Evening Prayer on Sundays and many feasts, and hear it at Mass; in Latin it is known as Laudate pueri, and it has been set to music for Vespers by many composers.

original.note: Latin: praise, O servants (or children), the psalm's first words and its name at Vespers.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general line of praise.
what it means: praise running from sunrise to sunset, to a God who stoops from the heavens to the dump to lift the poor.
what a scholar hears: the psalm opens the Hallel sung at Passover, and many think it was part of the hymn sung after the Last Supper.

sources.ref: 1 Kings 2:8 in the Douay (1 Samuel 2:8); Luke 1:52–53

notes: Douay Psalm 112:1, 3, 7–8 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition.
Hebrew 'avdei YHWH' (servants of the Lord); Vulgate 'pueri'. Confirm.
Hallel (Psalms 113–118) sung at Passover; the 'hymn' of Matthew 26:30 is commonly identified with part of the Hallel, hedged 'many think'.
Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:8) closely parallels Psalm 113:7–8. Confirm.
Placement of Psalm 113 in the Liturgy of the Hours (Sunday Evening Prayer in some weeks, and on feasts) is stated generally in howItsDone; a Keeper should confirm the exact weeks.
The dunghill as the town refuse heap where the destitute lived: common explanation; confirm.
